newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-METS REPLACE MCILVAINE AS GENERAL MANAGER.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-METS REPLACE MCILVAINE AS GENERAL MANAGER.

text.p: The New York Mets have been one of the most surprisingly good teams in baseball this season, but Wednesday they replaced general manager Joe McIlvaine, who built the current club.
Steve Phillips, 34, was promoted from assistant general manager to fill McIlvaine's position.

"We made this decision two or three weeks ago, but with the team on the road, we just didn't want to bring Joe back, so we waited for now," said Mets president and CEO Fred Wilpon said. "Our goal is to affect better results, not only this year, but in years to come.
"We have offered a major position in this organisation to Joe McIlvaine," Wilpon continued. "Joe is terrific at the acquisition of players and judging player development. That's what he likes to do.

Joe is where he likes to be and is very good and is very effective. He said he would seriously consider it. We hope very much Joe will accept this position," Wilpon said. "We ware trying to tailor our baseball department to the talents of the people we have."
Phillips said: "I can only hope Joe McIlvaine will accept our offer to stay with the organisation ... as a 34-year-old general manager, I can not possibley have all the answeres."
There was speculation that that McIlvaine's erratic behaviour and his work eithic prompted the change.
"I can't give you an exact one thing, but it was clear to Nelson (co-owner Nelson Doubleday) and me that Joe's absence from the big-league club was a factor," Wilpon said.
"He was working at what he loves to do," Wilpon said, citing McIlvaine's decision in May to attend the Florida high school baseball championships.
"He was the happiest man I've ever seen, watching those kids and projecting where they were going to be," he added.
Wilpon also dismissed suggestions that manager Bobby Valentine lobbied for today's changes.
"This decision was not pushed by Bobby Valentine. He did not know about this restructuring plan until after I talked to Joe today."

Late last season, as the club was winding down to a fourth-place finish in the National League East with a record of 71-91 (.438), McIlvaine hired Bobby Valentine to manage the team. The club has responded this year, going 51-41 (.554) for the league's fourth-best record.
The Mets started play on Wednesday third in the East, 7 1/2 games behind first-place Atlanta and 2 1/2 games behind second-place Florida, which holds the wild card spot.

Despite injuries that have sidelined all three of their young pitching prospects -- Paul Wilson, Jason Isringhausen and Bill Pulsipher -- the Mets have gone 24-25 on the road, a vast improvement from last year's 29-52 mark away from Shea Stadium.
In the offseason, McIlvaine acquired reliever Greg McMichael, starter Armando Reynoso and first baseman John Olerud, all of whom have been keys to New York's success in 1997.

McIlvaine also gutted the team of the malcontents in the locker room when he took over on July 8th, 1993, getting rid of high-priced underachievers Bobby Bonilla, Bret Saberhagen, Vince Coleman, Eddie Murray, Dwight Gooden and Tony Fernandez.
Phillips was named assitant GM in 1995 after serving as minor-league director the previous four seasons.
"Steve is in charge, he's the boss," Wilpon said. "Joe, as well as everyone else in the organisation, will report to him. The business has changed dramatically. One person can't do it all."

Phillips was a fifth-round draft choice of the Mets in 1981 and played in the organisation until getting traded to the Detroit Tigers in 1987. He retired as a player the following year and became an administrative assistant of scouting and minor leagues for the Mets in January 1990.
